Creditable means deserving of praise, respect, or acknowledgment. When you call something creditable, you are saying it is good enough — or better than good enough — to earn recognition and admiration.

Think of it this way: if someone "deserves credit" for what they did, then what they did was creditable.

Creditable is a word of quiet, genuine approval. It doesn't scream brilliance or perfection — it says: "This is worthy of respect. This deserves to be acknowledged."

It is most commonly used when someone has done something well, especially under difficult conditions or against expectations. There is often an undertone of: "Given the circumstances, this was genuinely impressive and praiseworthy."

For example:

  • A young tennis player competing against a former champion loses, but played extremely well. → Her performance was creditable.
  • A small company competes in a market dominated by giants and holds its ground. → That is a creditable achievement.
  • A student with very limited resources writes a thorough, well-reasoned essay. → It is a creditable piece of work.

In each case, the thing being described earns genuine respect and commendation.
What creditable does NOT mean — critical distinctions

This is the most important section, because creditable is one of the most frequently confused words in English. It looks and sounds similar to several other words, but it means something entirely different from all of them.

Creditable ≠ Credible

This is the most common confusion.

  • Credible means believable or trustworthy. A credible witness is one you can believe. A credible threat is one that seems real and serious.
  • Creditable means praiseworthy or worthy of recognition. A creditable performance is one that deserves admiration.

These two words have almost nothing to do with each other in meaning, even though they look alike. Never use one when you mean the other.

✗ "She gave a credible performance at the concert." ← This would mean her performance was believable, which is a strange thing to say about a concert.
✓ "She gave a creditable performance at the concert." ← This means her performance was praiseworthy.

✗ "He is a creditable source of information." ← This would mean he deserves praise for being a source, which makes no sense here.
✓ "He is a credible source of information." ← This means he is trustworthy and believable.

Creditable ≠ Credulous

  • Credulous means too willing to believe things; gullible. A credulous person gets fooled easily because they believe almost anything.
  • Creditable has nothing to do with gullibility.

Creditable ≠ Discreditable

  • Discreditable is the direct opposite of creditable. It means bringing shame, disgrace, or loss of respect. A discreditable act is one that harms your reputation.

Creditable sits in an interesting position. It is a word of genuine, sincere praise — but it does not always mean exceptional or outstanding. Sometimes it simply means: good enough to deserve respect and recognition, even if not perfect or spectacular.

This is why you'll often see it in sentences like:

  • "It was a creditable effort, though there is room for improvement."
  • "The team put up a creditable showing against the tournament favourites."

In such sentences, the speaker is sincerely praising what was done, but is also gently acknowledging that it was perhaps not flawless. It is honest approval — not hollow flattery, and not faint praise either.

However, creditable can also simply describe something genuinely impressive without any qualification:

  • "She has had a long and creditable career in public service."

Here, it means her career is genuinely admirable and worthy of recognition — full stop.

Creditable is a moderately formal word. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • Written reviews or assessments ("a creditable debut novel")
  • Formal reports or evaluations ("the team delivered a creditable result")
  • Commentary on sports, arts, or professional performance ("a creditable display from the home side")

In casual everyday speech, people more often just say "impressive," "praiseworthy," "commendable," or "well done." But in writing, or in more formal spoken contexts, creditable is precise and elegant.

Creditable = worthy of praise and recognition; deserving of credit for what was done.

If something is creditable, it earns genuine respect and acknowledgment — it is the kind of thing people should rightly give you credit for.
